metadata.version: Update of the 2011 American Heart Association scientific statement
metadata.summary: This scientific statement updates the American Heart Association’s 2011 guidance on recognizing, diagnosing, and managing cerebral venous thrombosis. It addresses clinical presentation, predisposing factors, imaging, anticoagulation, endovascular treatment, and decompressive surgery, including care for patients whose neurological condition worsens or whose thrombus progresses despite medical treatment. It also considers pediatric patients, pregnancy and the puerperium, and vaccine-induced thrombosis.

target_population: patients with suspected or confirmed CVT
patients with progressive neurological deterioration or thrombus propagation despite medical therapy
women with CVT during pregnancy or the puerperium
women with a history of CVT considering future pregnancy

toxicities.incidence: In RE-SPECT CVT, major hemorrhage occurred in 1 (1.7% [95% CI, 0.0%–8.9%]) patient receiving dabigatran and 2 (3.3% [95% CI, 0.4%–11.5%]) patients receiving warfarin. In EINSTEIN-Jr, 1 child receiving standard anticoagulation had a major subdural bleed. In ACTION-CVT, the DOAC group had a lower risk of major hemorrhage than the VKA group (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.35 [95% CI, 0.15–0.82]), principally because intracerebral hemorrhage was less frequent.
recognition: The RE-SPECT CVT event in the dabigatran group was gastrointestinal bleeding; both events in the warfarin group were intracerebral hemorrhages.
The major bleed reported with standard anticoagulation in EINSTEIN-Jr was subdural.

toxicities.incidence: In SECRET, by 6 months, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage occurred in 1 patient in the rivaroxaban group (3.8% [95% CI, 0.1%–19.6%]); no bleeding events occurred in the control group.

In SECRET, by 6 months, 2 patients in the rivaroxaban group had clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (7.7% [95% CI, 0.9%–25.1%]); no bleeding events occurred in the control group. In EINSTEIN-Jr, 5 children receiving rivaroxaban had nonmajor, noncerebral bleeding.

recognition: A reduced platelet count may identify thrombocytopenia.
prevention: For acute CVT treatment, LMWH is favored over unfractionated heparin in part because its thrombocytopenia risk is lower.

toxicities.event: Fetal embryopathy and fetal or neonatal bleeding
prevention: VKAs, including warfarin, are contraindicated during pregnancy because of these fetal and neonatal risks.

toxicities.event: Recurrent thromboembolic events in antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

toxicities.incidence: A pharmacovigilance study reported a disproportionately lower incident risk of CVT after mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccines than after adenovirus-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccines: 1–5/10000 for BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 versus 13/10000 for ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine. Initial cohorts of VITT with CVT reported mortality ranging from 39% to 61%; these figures are not the incidence of VITT.
recognition: Symptoms began 5 to 24 days after vaccination in the reported cases; headache was the most frequent presenting symptom.
Testing for platelet factor 4 antibodies is recommended when VITT is suspected.

management.actions: Expert hematology and multidisciplinary management is required. Despite limited evidence, avoidance of heparin products, intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg body weight daily for 2 days, and steroids have been advised. Platelet transfusions are not recommended. Nonheparin parenteral anticoagulants, such as argatroban or fondaparinux, are typically given first, with a switch to an oral anticoagulant such as DOAC after full platelet count recovery.

toxicities.incidence: A systematic review of 10 studies comprising 339 patients who underwent EVT for CVT reported a complication rate of 10.3%.

prophylaxis.recommendation: LMWH prophylaxis during a future pregnancy and the postpartum period is usually recommended for women with a history of CVT; the statement also describes it as probably beneficial.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women with a history of CVT during future pregnancies and the postpartum period
prophylaxis.duration: During future pregnancies and the postpartum period

therapies_index.name: unfractionated heparin

therapies_index.name: VKAs
approved_indications: Oral anticoagulation after initial parenteral treatment for CVT
therapies_index.administration: Earlier guidelines describe treatment for 3 to 12 months when risk factors are transient, or indefinitely with major chronic thrombosis risk factors or recurrent VTE. For CVT associated with pregnancy, LMWH or VKA with a target international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 is continued for at least 6 weeks postpartum, for a total minimum treatment duration of 3 months.

therapies_index.name: warfarin

therapies_index.administration: In RE-SPECT CVT, the target international normalized ratio was 2.0 to 3.0 after 5 to 15 days of initial parenteral anticoagulation, with treatment for 6 months.
key_toxicities: Associated with fetal embryopathy and bleeding in the fetus and neonate; contraindicated during pregnancy.
In RE-SPECT CVT, 2 (3.3% [95% CI, 0.4%–11.5%]) participants in the warfarin group had major hemorrhages, both intracerebral.

key_toxicities: Compared with warfarin, higher risks of recurrent thromboembolic events have been associated with DOACs in individuals with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with acute CVT, including those with venous hemorrhage
decision_rules: Begin parenteral anticoagulation for acute CVT; venous hemorrhage alone does not preclude it.
LMWH is favored over unfractionated heparin for initial treatment.
After initial parenteral treatment, transition to oral anticoagulation.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH followed by VKAs
recommended_regimens.summary: This is the established initial-to-oral anticoagulation approach described by the statement. LMWH is favored acutely because administration is more practical, its anticoagulant effect is more predictable, and thrombocytopenia is less likely. Meta-analyses show trends toward better outcomes that do not reach statistical significance.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 3 to 12 months when risk factors are transient; indefinitely when major chronic thrombotic risk factors or recurrent VTE are present

alternative_regimens.name: unfractionated heparin followed by VKAs
alternative_regimens.summary: Unfractionated heparin is an initial parenteral anticoagulant option, although LMWH is favored.

response_assessment.method: CTV or MRV assessment of venous recanalization
response_assessment.interpretation: Whether recanalization should determine anticoagulation duration remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Anticoagulation aims to limit thrombus extension, promote recanalization, and prevent recurrent VTE.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with CVT and a transient risk factor who have completed initial parenteral anticoagulation
decision_rules: Use the transient nature of the provoking factor when selecting the duration of oral anticoagulation.
The value of using subsequent venous recanalization to determine treatment duration is uncertain.

recommended_regimens.name: VKAs
recommended_regimens.summary: Continue oral anticoagulation after initial parenteral treatment when the underlying risk factor is transient.

alternative_regimens.name: DOAC
alternative_regimens.summary: Transition to a DOAC is reasonable for selected patients after initial parenteral anticoagulation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Patient selection must account for the restrictions described for pregnancy, breastfeeding, and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

response_assessment.method: CTV or MRV assessment of venous recanalization
response_assessment.interpretation: Using the degree of recanalization to set anticoagulation duration remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with CVT and major chronic risk factors for thrombosis or recurrent VTE
decision_rules: Major chronic thrombotic risk factors or recurrent VTE support indefinite oral anticoagulation after initial parenteral treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: VKAs
recommended_regimens.summary: Continue oral anticoagulation after parenteral heparin when major chronic thrombotic risk factors or recurrent VTE are present.

response_assessment.method: CTV or MRV assessment of venous recanalization
response_assessment.interpretation: Its role in deciding anticoagulation duration is uncertain.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: DOACs have been associated with a higher risk of recurrent thromboembolic events than warfarin in individuals with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected patients with CVT transitioning from initial parenteral anticoagulation to oral treatment
decision_rules: A transition to either DOAC or VKA after lead-in parenteral anticoagulation is reasonable.
It is unknown whether 5 to 15 days of parenteral lead-in is safer or more effective than a shorter period.
The optimal timing of DOAC initiation, need for initial acute VTE dosing, and best candidates for DOAC treatment remain unsettled.

recommended_regimens.name: DOAC
recommended_regimens.summary: DOACs appear to offer a safe and effective oral alternative to VKAs for selected patients. ACTION-CVT found no significant difference in recurrent VTE between DOAC and VKA groups and found less major hemorrhage in the DOAC group; these are observational study findings.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In ACTION-CVT, recurrent VTE had an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.94 [95% CI, 0.15– 1.73] and major hemorrhage had an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.35 [95% CI, 0.15–0.82] for DOAC versus VKA. A systematic review reported complete recanalization of 42.9% versus 42.3%; relative risk, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87–1.11] for DOACs versus VKAs.

alternative_regimens.name: VKAs
alternative_regimens.summary: VKA remains a reasonable oral anticoagulation choice after initial parenteral treatment.

not_recommended.name: DOAC
not_recommended.reason: DOACs are contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding. In antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, they have been associated with higher recurrent thromboembolic risk than warfarin.

response_assessment.method: CTV or MRV assessment of venous recanalization
response_assessment.interpretation: Whether this finding should guide treatment duration is uncertain.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The oral anticoagulants reported in ACTION-CVT included apixaban (67%), rivaroxaban (18%), dabigatran (14%), and multiple DOACs (3%). The study excluded individuals with malignancy, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, or pregnancy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with CVT eligible for the oral anticoagulation approaches examined in RE-SPECT CVT or SECRET
decision_rules: Interpret the named drug approaches in light of their respective trial eligibility criteria rather than assuming that every patient with CVT was represented.

alternative_regimens.name: dabigatran
alternative_regimens.summary: RE-SPECT CVT studied dabigatran 150 mg twice daily for 6 months after 5 to 15 days of parenteral anticoagulation against warfarin with a target international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0. Neither group had recurrent VTE; major hemorrhage occurred in 1 (1.7% [95% CI, 0.0%–8.9%]) participant receiving dabigatran and 2 (3.3% [95% CI, 0.4%–11.5%]) receiving warfarin.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The trial excluded individuals with malignancy, central nervous system infection, trauma, or pregnancy.

alternative_regimens.name: rivaroxaban
alternative_regimens.summary: SECRET studied rivaroxaban 20 mg daily against standard anticoagulation for a minimum of 6 months. By 6 months, the rivaroxaban group had 1 recurrent CVT (3.8% [95% CI, 0.1%–19.6%]), 1 symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (3.8% [95% CI, 0.1%–19.6%]), and 2 clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding events (7.7% [95% CI, 0.9%–25.1%]); the control group had no VTE recurrence or bleeding events.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: SECRET excluded individuals with pregnancy or antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Parenteral lead-in was not required, although 19 of 26 participants receiving rivaroxaban had ≤4 days of parenteral lead-in.

response_assessment.method: Recurrent VTE and bleeding assessment in RE-SPECT CVT and SECRET
response_assessment.interpretation: The results apply to the respective trial groups and eligibility criteria.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: These are reported trial regimens and outcomes, not separate preferential recommendations for dabigatran or rivaroxaban over other DOACs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with thrombus propagation, neurological deterioration despite medical therapy, failure of standard therapy, or a contraindication to anticoagulation
decision_rules: Reserve endovascular therapy for the specified rescue circumstances rather than routine treatment of an unselected CVT population.
Available evidence does not establish one endovascular technique as superior.

recommended_regimens.name: EVT
recommended_regimens.summary: Endovascular treatment is reserved as a rescue approach when standard medical treatment fails, clinical status deteriorates, thrombus extends, or anticoagulation is contraindicated. Techniques reported include mechanical thrombectomy, intrasinus thrombolysis, their combination, intra-arterial thrombolysis, and intrasinus stenting.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: TO-ACT found no clinical benefit from EVT over standard anticoagulation in severe CVT. Larger studies and meta-analyses reported higher mortality and no evidence of benefit with EVT. A systematic review of 10 studies comprising 339 patients undergoing EVT reported complete or partial postoperative recanalization in 90.0%, rising to 95.2% during follow-up, and a complication rate of 10.3%.

not_recommended.name: EVT as routine treatment in an unselected CVT population
not_recommended.reason: A favorable outcome association is uncertain; TO-ACT showed no clinical benefit in severe CVT compared with standard anticoagulation, and larger studies and meta-analyses found higher mortality and no evidence of benefit.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence on the safety and complication rates of individual endovascular approaches is controversial.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with acute severe CVT, parenchymal lesions, and impending herniation
decision_rules: Offer decompressive craniectomy as a potentially lifesaving intervention when parenchymal lesions accompany impending herniation.

recommended_regimens.name: decompressive craniectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer decompressive surgery for acute severe CVT with impending herniation. No randomized controlled trials of this approach are reported.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 studies comprising 483 patients found that surgery within 48 hours of admission may reduce mortality (odds ratio [OR], 0.26 [95% CI, 0.10–0.69]) and improve functional outcomes.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: within 48 hours of admission in the cited analysis

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Factors associated with poorer outcomes included age >50 years, midline shift >10 mm, and total effacement of basal cisterns.

decision_rules: Use parenteral anticoagulation as initial treatment.
If consciousness deteriorates, consider more invasive procedures that may be lifesaving.
Follow initial parenteral treatment with LMWH, VKA, or rivaroxaban for at least 6 weeks.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH or unfractionated heparin followed by LMWH, VKA, or rivaroxaban
recommended_regimens.summary: Acute pediatric treatment generally begins with LMWH or unfractionated heparin, followed by one of the listed anticoagulation options.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In Kids-DOTT, 6 weeks of anticoagulation was noninferior to 3 months for recurrent VTE and bleeding events among children with provoked VTE, a study that included patients with CVT.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The pediatric evidence discussed includes trials of anticoagulation duration and rivaroxaban after initial heparinization.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Premature and term neonates with acute CVT
decision_rules: Acute anticoagulation is more controversial in neonates than in older children, but it is reasonable because untreated thrombus may propagate and evidence of posttreatment hemorrhage is lacking.
Consider more invasive procedures if consciousness deteriorates.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH or unfractionated heparin
recommended_regimens.summary: Parenteral anticoagulation is a reasonable acute approach in premature and term neonates despite greater uncertainty in this age group.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with confirmed CVT after initial heparinization
decision_rules: Rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulation were the post-heparinization options examined in EINSTEIN-Jr.

alternative_regimens.name: rivaroxaban
alternative_regimens.summary: In EINSTEIN-Jr, children received rivaroxaban for 3 months after initial heparinization. Symptomatic recurrent VTE occurred in none of the 73 children receiving rivaroxaban versus 1 of the 41 receiving standard anticoagulation (absolute difference, 2.4% [95% CI, −2.6% to 13.5%]). Five rivaroxaban recipients had nonmajor, noncerebral bleeding.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Studied in children with confirmed CVT after initial heparinization.

alternative_regimens.name: continuing heparin or switching to oral VKAs
alternative_regimens.summary: These approaches formed the standard-anticoagulation comparator in EINSTEIN-Jr. One child receiving standard anticoagulation had a major subdural bleed.

response_assessment.timepoint: end of the 3-month study treatment period
response_assessment.method: Symptomatic recurrent VTE, bleeding, venous recanalization, focal neurological deficits, and survival in EINSTEIN-Jr
response_assessment.interpretation: No children died. Complete or partial recanalization occurred in 18 (25%) and 39 (53%) children receiving rivaroxaban, respectively, and 6 (15%) and 24 (59%) receiving standard anticoagulation, respectively. Focal neurological deficits were observed in 5 (6.8%) and 3 (7.3%) children in the respective groups.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Longer-term studies suggest that, despite treatment, 1 in 4 children may develop late epilepsy, infantile spasms after neonatal CVT, cognitive impairment, or intracranial hypertension.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with CVT during pregnancy and early puerperium
decision_rules: Continue full-dose LMWH throughout pregnancy.
After delivery, continue LMWH or transition to VKA at the specified international normalized ratio for the stated postpartum and total treatment durations.
Reserve thrombolysis or thrombectomy for neurological deterioration or thrombus propagation despite medical treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH
recommended_regimens.summary: Use LMWH at full anticoagulant doses throughout pregnancy; LMWH can also be continued postpartum.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: throughout pregnancy and for at least 6 weeks postpartum, with a total minimum duration of therapy of 3 months

recommended_regimens.name: VKA
recommended_regimens.summary: A postpartum continuation option, with a target international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0; VKAs are contraindicated during pregnancy.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: at least 6 weeks postpartum, with a total minimum duration of therapy of 3 months

alternative_regimens.name: thrombolysis or thrombectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: These interventions are reserved for rescue circumstances; evidence in this population is limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Neurological deterioration or thrombus propagation despite medical therapy.

not_recommended.name: VKAs, including warfarin, during pregnancy
not_recommended.reason: They are contraindicated because of fetal embryopathy and bleeding in the fetus and neonate.

not_recommended.name: DOAC during pregnancy
not_recommended.reason: DOACs are contraindicated during pregnancy; the statement recommends only LMWH for pregnant women.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with CVT who are breastfeeding and require oral anticoagulation
decision_rules: Do not use DOACs during breastfeeding.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with a history of CVT during a future pregnancy and postpartum period
decision_rules: Advise that a prior CVT does not contraindicate future pregnancy.
LMWH prophylaxis during future pregnancies and the postpartum period is usually recommended; the statement also describes it as probably beneficial.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide prophylaxis in a future pregnancy and postpartum period after prior CVT.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A systematic review of 17 studies and 393 pregnancies reported recurrent CVT at 8 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 3–22) and noncerebral VTE at 22 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 11–43). It reported a trend toward fewer recurrent thrombotic events among women receiving antithrombotic prophylaxis.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: during future pregnancies and the postpartum period

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited review reports a trend, rather than a demonstrated reduction, in recurrent thrombotic events with prophylaxis.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with suspected VITT and CVT
decision_rules: Test for platelet factor 4 antibodies when VITT is suspected.
Obtain management from a hematologist and multidisciplinary team.
Avoid heparin products; use a nonheparin parenteral anticoagulant initially and transition to oral anticoagulation after full platelet count recovery.

recommended_regimens.name: argatroban or fondaparinux followed by DOAC
recommended_regimens.summary: A nonheparin parenteral anticoagulant is typically used first, followed by an oral anticoagulant such as DOAC once platelet counts have fully recovered.

not_recommended.name: heparin products
not_recommended.reason: Avoidance has been advised because VITT resembles autoimmune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, despite a lack of evidence for this approach.

not_recommended.name: platelet transfusions
not_recommended.reason: They are not recommended in suspected VITT.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before transition from parenteral to oral anticoagulation
response_assessment.interpretation: Transition once the platelet count has fully recovered.

supportive_care: Intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg body weight daily for 2 days and steroids have been advised despite a lack of evidence.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The statement calls for expert hematology and multidisciplinary management.

conditions.name: CVT
conditions.description: A thrombus affects the dural venous sinuses, cerebral veins, or both. Predisposing conditions may be transient or chronic. Reported factors include oral contraception, pregnancy or the puerperium, hormonal therapy, obesity, infections, dehydration, anemia, autoimmune disease, malignancy, thrombophilia, head trauma, neurosurgical procedures, and lesions compressing a venous sinus.
conditions.epidemiology: CVT accounts for 0.5% to 3% of strokes. Registry and cohort data suggest that affected people are predominantly <55 years of age and that two-thirds are women. Rates are highest among younger women. Estrogen-based oral contraception and hormonal therapies may increase the odds of CVT nearly 8-fold, with a possible additional interaction with obesity.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms may arise from raised intracranial pressure or focal parenchymal injury, with or without mass effect. Headache occurs in nearly 90% of cases. Other manifestations include nausea, transient visual obscurations or vision loss (13%–27%), papilledema, diplopia (6%–14%), and other cranial neuropathies (6%–11%). Seizures occur at presentation in approximately 20% to 40%, focal neurological deficits in 20% to 50%, and encephalopathy or coma in up to 20%. Onset is generally more gradual than in other stroke types; the majority present >48 hours after symptom onset. A minority present acutely with thunderclap headache or subarachnoid hemorrhage (<5%) or an abrupt focal neurological deficit (5%–40%).

subtypes.name: cortical vein thrombosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Small cortical venous thrombi can be inconspicuous and require particular attention to contrast-enhanced or susceptibility-sensitive imaging.

subtypes.name: deep cerebral vein thrombosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Deep venous involvement may produce bilateral parenchymal abnormalities; the illustrated findings include bilateral thalamic signal changes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess an acute presentation for a visible thrombus and the tissue consequences of venous obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Often obtained initially when symptoms are nonspecific.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A hyperattenuating thrombus may produce a dense vessel sign. A cord or string sign or dense triangle sign can persist up to 14 days after symptom onset. Suspicious indirect findings include hypodensities that do not follow an arterial territory, bilateral abnormalities, and hemorrhage. Hemorrhages occur in up to 40% of CVT cases. In a meta-analysis of 27 publications with 2812 cases, CT sensitivity was 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity was 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify venous thrombus and associated parenchymal injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used in the initial assessment and alongside venous imaging to establish the diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Thrombus signal changes with age on T1 and T2 sequences; early thrombosis may resemble a normal venous flow void. MRI is more sensitive than CT for parenchymal lesions caused by venous occlusion, which may cross arterial territories or be bilateral. A meta-analysis of 21 studies with 1773 patients with CVT reported sensitivity of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity of 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94) for conventional MRI sequences.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm CVT by depicting the superficial and deep cerebral venous systems.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An optimal confirmatory test and a reasonable alternative to MRI/MRV where resources are limited or pretest probability is low.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Thrombi appear as venous filling defects. CTV is less sensitive than MRI for cortical vein thrombosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm thrombosis in the cerebral venous system.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: MRI/MRV is the recommended noninvasive confirmatory study.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Venous filling abnormalities must be assessed with awareness that flow-dependent techniques can produce artifacts or flow gaps.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess luminal filling directly and improve detection of thrombus in smaller veins.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Useful when findings from noncontrast sequences require corroboration and recommended for diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its sensitivity and specificity are comparable to those of CTV; it better distinguishes a low-flow state from a hypoplastic sinus.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Image cerebral venous flow without contrast.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly useful when gadolinium administration may be precluded, including pregnancy, breastfeeding, or severe renal failure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Complex flow can cause artifacts, and absent flow may not be corroborated by T1 or T2 findings. Compared with 3-dimensional TOF, 2-dimensional TOF is more sensitive when flow is slow.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide noncontrast venous imaging.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Complex flow can cause artifacts. Its use is less frequent because selection of the velocity-encoding parameter is difficult and operator dependent, and acquisition takes longer.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Corroborate suspected venous thrombus through susceptibility-related findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Helpful when conventional MRI or flow-dependent MRV is uncertain; recommended for diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact, particularly useful for identifying cortical venous thrombi.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Corroborate venous thrombosis, including subtle cortical venous thrombi.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Helpful when conventional findings are uncertain; recommended for diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Thrombus produces susceptibility-related signal changes. For thrombosed cortical veins, the reported sensitivity and specificity approach 100%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Depict thrombus while suppressing signal from flowing blood.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Described as a promising advanced MRI technique.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate cerebral venous anatomy when an invasive intervention is being considered.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Typically reserved for consideration of invasive treatment.

long_term_effects: Residual headache, fatigue, low mood, and cognitive difficulties may persist despite functional independence and may hinder a return to previous activities.

Epilepsy may affect >10% of individuals with CVT; reported risk factors include seizures at onset, reduced consciousness or focal deficits, initial hemorrhagic lesions, superior sagittal sinus involvement, and craniectomy.
Dural arteriovenous fistula can develop after CVT, although CVT can also follow a dural arteriovenous fistula.
Recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) after CVT has a reported incidence of 1% to 4% per year; recurrence of CVT is generally reported as <1% to 2% per year.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Overall, 80% to 90% of patients achieve functional independence, defined as a modified Rankin Scale score of 0–2, but persistent symptoms can affect quality of life. Death or dependence occurs in 10% to 15% despite intensive medical treatment. A study of 303 previously employed patients or students found that 42% had not returned to work or school at 6 months, although 87% were functionally independent when assessed. Using subsequent CTV or MRV recanalization to determine anticoagulation duration remains uncertain.

conditions.name: cortical vein thrombosis
conditions.description: Thrombosis affecting cortical cerebral veins; its imaging findings may be less conspicuous than thrombosis of larger venous structures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect cortical venous thrombus through direct assessment of venous filling.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended when diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Contrast enhancement improves detection of thrombi in smaller veins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Reveal small thrombosed cortical veins.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended when diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A susceptibility-related blooming artifact can make an otherwise subtle thrombus apparent; reported sensitivity and specificity approach 100% for thrombosed cortical veins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Reveal small thrombosed cortical veins.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended when diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Susceptibility-related findings help identify subtle cortical venous thrombi; reported sensitivity and specificity approach 100%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess cerebral venous filling.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its sensitivity for cortical vein thrombosis is lower than that of MRI.

conditions.name: CVT in children
conditions.description: Pediatric CVT is discussed in association with sepsis, head trauma, hypoxia, dehydration, congenital heart disease and its surgical treatment, cancer and its treatment, iron deficiency or hemoglobinopathy-related anemia, and inflammatory conditions.
conditions.epidemiology: CVT is more common in neonates (6.4/100000) than in older children and adolescents. Mortality among children with CVT is 3%, and recurrent venous thrombosis occurs in ≈6%; recurrence is usually associated with absence of anticoagulation and lack of venous recanalization.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute manifestations that should prompt consideration of CVT include headache, seizures, focal neurological deficits, and coma. Relevant clinical contexts include infections such as mastoiditis, Lemierre syndrome, COVID-19, or meningitis, as well as trauma, hypoxia, and dehydration.

subtypes.name: CVT in neonates
subtypes.distinguishing_features: CVT is more common in neonates than in other pediatric age groups, and the guide describes acute anticoagulation in premature and term neonates as more controversial.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Diagnose or exclude dural or cortical venous thrombosis and assess accompanying parenchymal involvement or hemorrhage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In children with a compatible acute presentation or predisposing circumstances.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The examination typically requires anesthesia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify platelet, hemoglobin, and iron-deficiency abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the initial pediatric assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low platelet counts may accompany platelet factor 4 mutations; elevated platelets and hemoglobin may accompany JAK2 mutations. Iron-deficiency indices may be present with or without anemia.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: The pediatric assessment notes a possible association with low platelet counts.
The pediatric assessment notes a possible association with elevated platelet counts and hemoglobin.

long_term_effects: Longer-term studies suggest that, despite treatment, 1 in 4 children may develop late epilepsy, infantile spasms after neonatal CVT, cognitive impairment, or intracranial hypertension.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: In the EINSTEIN-Jr trial, focal neurological deficits remained at the end of the 3-month treatment period in 5 (6.8%) children receiving rivaroxaban and 3 (7.3%) receiving standard anticoagulation. No children died by the end of that treatment period.

conditions.name: CVT in neonates
conditions.description: Neonatal CVT is distinguished within the pediatric population by its greater frequency and by uncertainty surrounding anticoagulation during the acute phase in premature and term neonates.
conditions.epidemiology: The reported frequency in neonates is 6.4/100000, higher than in children and adolescents.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish or exclude dural or cortical venous thrombosis and identify associated parenchymal injury or hemorrhage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In a pediatric acute presentation in which CVT is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Imaging in children typically requires anesthesia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess platelet count, hemoglobin, and evidence of iron deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the initial pediatric assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low platelets may be associated with platelet factor 4 mutations; high platelets and hemoglobin may be associated with JAK2 mutations. Iron deficiency may occur with or without anemia.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: The pediatric discussion associates these mutations with potentially low platelet counts on initial testing.
The pediatric discussion associates these mutations with potentially elevated platelets and hemoglobin on initial testing.

long_term_effects: Infantile spasms are reported among possible later outcomes after neonatal CVT.

conditions.name: CVT During Pregnancy and Puerperium
conditions.description: Pregnancy-related changes in coagulation continue into the puerperium and create a hypercoagulable state associated with CVT. The greatest-risk intervals are the third trimester and the first 6 postpartum weeks.
conditions.epidemiology: Estimates for pregnancy and the puerperium range from 1 in 2500 deliveries to 1 in 10000 deliveries in Western countries, with reported ORs from 1.3 to 13.0. Approximately 80% of pregnancy-related cases occur after delivery. A case-control study found increased risk confined to the puerperium (OR, 10.6 [95% CI, 5.6–20.0]); the increase during pregnancy was not statistically significant (OR, 1.2 [95% CI, 0.6–2.3]). Cesarean delivery appeared associated with higher risk after adjustment for specified factors (OR, 3.10 [95% CI, 2.26–4.24]).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Image the cerebral venous system without gadolinium.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Useful when gadolinium administration may be precluded during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Flow-dependent artifacts can complicate interpretation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm suspected CVT noninvasively.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended as the noninvasive confirmatory study for CVT.

long_term_effects: Women with a history of VTE appear to face increased thrombotic risk in subsequent pregnancies. A systematic review of 17 studies and 393 pregnancies reported CVT recurrence of 8 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 3–22) and noncerebral VTE of 22 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 11–43).
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Studies published since the earlier statement describe prognosis after pregnancy-related CVT as better than or similar to prognosis for CVT overall. The statement says prior CVT is not a contraindication to a future pregnancy.

conditions.name: VITT and CVT
conditions.description: A rare presentation involving thrombocytopenia and CVT after adenovirus-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. The statement describes a proposed process in which DNA from adenovirus-infected cells binds platelet factor 4 and induces autoantibodies.
conditions.epidemiology: Reports after ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine and Ad26.COV2.S described affected individuals aged 18 to 77 years, most of them women. Initial cohort studies reported mortality ranging from 39% to 61%. A pharmacovigilance study reported a disproportionately lower incident CVT risk after mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccines than after adenovirus-based vaccines (1–5/10000 for BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 versus 13/10000 for ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine); it found no evidence of VITT after mRNA vaccines.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms began 5 to 24 days after vaccination. Headache was the most frequent presenting feature, and all reported patients had thrombocytopenia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected VITT.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended when VITT is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Antibodies to platelet factor 4 were reported in affected patients.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the thrombocytopenia associated with this presentation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When VITT and CVT are suspected after vaccination.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: All patients in the described reports had thrombocytopenia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm suspected CVT noninvasively.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended as the noninvasive confirmatory study for CVT.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide an alternative assessment for suspected CVT.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Reasonable where resources are limited or CVT pretest probability is low.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Testing is recommended when VITT is suspected; antibodies to platelet factor 4 were documented after ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccination in a reported patient series.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The statement describes VITT-associated CVT as rare but associated with poor prognosis in initial cohorts.

recommendations.statement: Maintain strong clinical suspicion for CVT when patients have compatible symptoms together with predisposing conditions such as pregnancy, puerperium, oral contraceptive use, or thrombophilia, or when they belong to a higher-risk demographic group such as young women.
recommendations.rationale: CVT has varied manifestations and can be difficult to recognize.

recommendations.statement: Use MRI/MRV as the recommended noninvasive examination of the cerebral venous system to confirm CVT; CT/CTV is a reasonable alternative where resources are limited or pretest probability is low.
For suspected cortical venous thrombosis, use contrast-enhanced MRV, gradient-recalled echo, or susceptibility-weighted imaging sequences.
recommendations.rationale: These techniques help identify thrombosed cortical veins.

recommendations.statement: Typically reserve digital subtraction angiography for situations in which an invasive treatment is being considered.

Treat CVT initially with parenteral heparin, then transition to oral VKAs for 3 to 12 months according to the underlying cause, or continue indefinitely when thrombophilia or recurrent VTE is present.
recommendations.rationale: Anticoagulation is intended to limit thrombus extension, facilitate recanalization, and prevent recurrent VTE.

recommendations.statement: For initial CVT treatment, previous American Heart Association/American Stroke Association and European guidelines recommend LMWH rather than unfractionated heparin.
recommendations.rationale: LMWH is easier to administer, has a more predictable anticoagulant effect and a lower thrombocytopenia risk; trends toward better outcomes in meta-analyses did not reach statistical significance.

recommendations.statement: Do not treat venous hemorrhage as a contraindication to anticoagulation for CVT.
DOACs appear to be a safe and effective alternative to VKAs for selected people with CVT; after initial parenteral anticoagulation, transition to either a DOAC or VKA is reasonable.
recommendations.context: The safest or most effective duration of initial parenteral treatment is not established.
recommendations.rationale: The statement cites open-label retrospective and prospective randomized studies, while noting that it is unknown whether 5 to 15 days of initial parenteral anticoagulation is safer or more effective than a shorter period.

recommendations.statement: Do not use DOACs during pregnancy or breastfeeding; during pregnancy, use LMWH rather than DOACs or warfarin.
recommendations.context: Pregnant or breastfeeding patients requiring anticoagulation for CVT
recommendations.rationale: The statement identifies DOACs and warfarin as contraindicated during pregnancy and DOACs as contraindicated during breastfeeding.

recommendations.statement: Carefully weigh potential benefits of aspirin after stopping oral anticoagulation against individual patient characteristics through shared decision-making.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence specifically addressing antiplatelet treatment after CVT is limited, and patients with CVT may face a longer lifetime exposure to aspirin.

recommendations.statement: Reserve endovascular therapies for CVT with thrombus propagation, neurological deterioration despite medical treatment, or a contraindication to anticoagulation.
recommendations.context: Rescue treatment rather than routine treatment
recommendations.rationale: Controlled evidence is lacking, and meta-analyses reported poorer outcomes; the TO-ACT trial did not show clinical benefit over standard anticoagulation in severe CVT.

recommendations.statement: Offer decompressive craniectomy as a potentially lifesaving treatment for acute severe CVT with parenchymal lesions and impending herniation.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence is limited, but surgery may improve functional outcomes in patients with advanced signs of herniation.

recommendations.statement: In children with acute CVT, use parenteral anticoagulation as first-line treatment, followed by LMWH, VKA, or rivaroxaban for at least 6 weeks.
Anticoagulation is reasonable for premature and term neonates with acute CVT, although its use in this population is more controversial.
recommendations.rationale: The statement reports no evidence of hemorrhage after treatment and notes that withholding anticoagulation may allow thrombus propagation.

recommendations.statement: Consider more invasive procedures for a child with CVT whose level of consciousness deteriorates.

For CVT during pregnancy, continue LMWH at full anticoagulant doses throughout pregnancy; continue LMWH or VKA with a target international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 for at least 6 weeks postpartum, for a total minimum treatment duration of 3 months.
For pregnancy-related CVT, reserve thrombolysis and thrombectomy for neurological deterioration or thrombus propagation despite medical treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence on endovascular therapies in this population is limited.

recommendations.statement: It is reasonable to advise women with previous CVT that a future pregnancy is not contraindicated; LMWH prophylaxis during future pregnancies and the postpartum period is usually recommended.
recommendations.rationale: Pregnancy adds thrombotic risk for women with a history of CVT, and prophylaxis is probably beneficial.

recommendations.statement: Obtain laboratory testing for platelet factor 4 antibodies when VITT is suspected.
For suspected VITT, avoidance of heparin products, intravenous immunoglobulin at 1 g/kg body weight daily for 2 days, and steroids have been advised.
recommendations.rationale: The advice is based on similarity to autoimmune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia despite a lack of evidence.

recommendations.statement: Do not give platelet transfusions for suspected VITT.

For suspected VITT, typically start with a nonheparin parenteral anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux, then transition to an oral anticoagulant such as a DOAC once the platelet count has fully recovered.
Arrange expert management by a hematologist and a multidisciplinary team for VITT-associated CVT.

artifacts.title: Proposed algorithm for the management of CVT
artifacts.source_heading: THERAPEUTIC ADVANCES IN THE MANAGEMENT OF CVT
artifacts.description: Step 1: If CVT is suspected, assess the cerebral venous system with MRI/MRV; CT/CTV is a reasonable alternative where resources are limited or pretest probability is low. Step 2: For confirmed CVT, begin parenteral heparin and then consider transition to oral anticoagulation according to the underlying cause and patient characteristics. Step 3: If thrombosis propagates, neurological status deteriorates despite medical treatment, or anticoagulation is contraindicated, reserve endovascular therapy as a rescue option. Step 4: If severe CVT with parenchymal lesions threatens herniation, offer decompressive craniectomy as a lifesaving intervention. The figure caption identifies the element as a proposed diagnostic and management algorithm but does not specify its intermediate branches; these steps reflect the accompanying clinical guidance.
artifacts.summary: The proposed algorithm addresses diagnostic confirmation and management of CVT, including escalation when a patient deteriorates or thrombus extends.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It connects confirmation of CVT with initial anticoagulation and identifies situations requiring consideration of invasive treatment.

artifacts.title: KEY POINTS FOR CLINICAL PRACTICE
artifacts.description: Clinical practice points: Maintain strong suspicion for CVT when common symptoms accompany recognized risks, including pregnancy, puerperium, oral contraceptive use, thrombophilia, or young age in women. The statement additionally identifies obesity, COVID-19, and vaccine-induced thrombocytopenia as predisposing conditions. Use MRI/MRV to confirm CVT noninvasively; CT/CTV is a reasonable alternative with limited resources or low pretest probability. For cortical venous thrombosis, use contrast-enhanced MRV, gradient-recalled echo, or susceptibility-weighted imaging. Start with parenteral heparin, then transition to oral VKAs for 3 to 12 months according to the cause, or continue indefinitely with thrombophilia or recurrent VTE. DOACs appear to offer a safe and effective alternative to VKAs on the basis of the cited open-label retrospective and prospective randomized studies. Whether subsequent CTV or MRV evidence of recanalization should determine anticoagulation duration remains uncertain. Reserve endovascular treatment for thrombus propagation, neurological deterioration despite medical treatment, or contraindications to anticoagulation; controlled studies are lacking, and meta-analyses report poorer outcomes. Decompressive surgery may save life and improve function when advanced signs of herniation are present, although evidence is limited. For CVT during pregnancy, continue full-dose LMWH throughout pregnancy, followed by LMWH or VKA at a target international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 for at least 6 weeks postpartum, with a total treatment duration of at least 3 months. Advise that prior CVT does not contraindicate a future pregnancy; LMWH prophylaxis during a future pregnancy and postpartum is usually recommended. For pediatric CVT, use parenteral anticoagulation first, followed by LMWH, VKA, or rivaroxaban for at least 6 weeks. Rare VITT-associated CVT after adenovirus-based SARSCoV-2 vaccination warrants management by a hematologist and a multidisciplinary team.
artifacts.summary: This set of practice points brings together diagnostic, anticoagulation, escalation, pregnancy, pediatric, and VITT-related guidance. It also distinguishes emerging options from questions that remain unresolved.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It provides a concise reference for selecting imaging, initiating treatment, recognizing when escalation is warranted, and adapting care for specific populations.
