special_populations.considerations: CVT is more frequent in neonates (6.4/100000) than in older children. In children with headache, seizures, focal neurological deficits, or coma, the diagnosis warrants early consideration, particularly with sepsis, head trauma, hypoxia, or dehydration. Relevant preexisting conditions include congenital heart disease, cancer, iron deficiency, hemoglobinopathies, and inflammatory disease. Emergency imaging may require anesthesia. Initial blood tests may show platelet or hemoglobin abnormalities associated with platelet factor 4 or JAK2 mutations, or evidence of iron deficiency. Pediatric CVT has a mortality rate of 3%, and recurrent venous thrombosis occurs in ≈6%. Later epilepsy, cognitive impairment, or intracranial hypertension can occur despite treatment. In Kids-DOTT, 6 weeks of anticoagulation was noninferior to 3 months for recurrent VTE and bleeding in children with provoked VTE, including CVT. In EINSTEIN-Jr, none of the 73 children receiving rivaroxaban and 1 of the 41 receiving standard anticoagulation had symptomatic recurrent VTE during the 3-month treatment period.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Acute treatment generally uses LMWH or unfractionated heparin. If consciousness deteriorates, more invasive procedures should be considered. Anticoagulation in premature and term neonates is more controversial but is considered reasonable. Parenteral anticoagulation is first-line, followed by LMWH, VKA, or rivaroxaban for at least 6 weeks. In EINSTEIN-Jr, children received initial heparinization before 3 months of rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulation.

special_populations.considerations: Pregnancy-related changes in coagulation persist after delivery. Estimated CVT incidence during pregnancy and the puerperium ranges from 1 in 2500 deliveries to 1 in 10000 deliveries in Western countries; the highest-risk periods are the third trimester and first 6 postpartum weeks. Approximately 80% of pregnancy-related cases occur after delivery. One case-control study found increased risk only during the puerperium (OR, 10.6 [95% CI, 5.6–20.0]); the increase during pregnancy was not statistically significant (OR, 1.2 [95% CI, 0.6–2.3]). Cesarean delivery appeared associated with greater risk after adjustment (OR, 3.10 [95% CI, 2.26–4.24]). Studies published since the earlier statement found outcomes for pregnancy-related CVT to be at least as favorable as those for CVT overall.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: During pregnancy, DOAC and warfarin are contraindicated; LMWH is the recommended anticoagulant. Full anticoagulant doses of LMWH should continue throughout pregnancy. For at least 6 weeks postpartum, LMWH or VKA with a target international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 should continue, for a total minimum treatment duration of 3 months. Evidence for endovascular treatment in this population is limited; thrombolysis or thrombectomy is reserved for neurological deterioration or thrombus propagation despite medical treatment.

special_populations.population: Women with a history of CVT considering future pregnancies
special_populations.considerations: A previous CVT does not contraindicate another pregnancy. Women with a history of VTE appear to face greater thrombotic risk in subsequent pregnancies. A systematic review of 17 studies and 393 pregnancies reported recurrent CVT at 8 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 3–22) and noncerebral VTE at 22 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 11–43). Antithrombotic prophylaxis showed a trend toward fewer recurrent thrombotic events.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Women can reasonably be advised that future pregnancy is not contraindicated. LMWH prophylaxis during a future pregnancy and the postpartum period is described as probably beneficial and is usually recommended.

special_populations.considerations: Breastfeeding affects the choice of oral anticoagulant and, when gadolinium administration is to be avoided, venous imaging technique.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: DOACs are contraindicated during breastfeeding. TOF MRV can be useful when gadolinium administration is precluded.

special_populations.considerations: VITT-associated CVT has been reported after the adenovirus-based ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine and Ad26.COV2.S vaccine. Reported symptoms began 5 to 24 days after vaccination; headache was the most common presenting symptom, and affected patients had thrombocytopenia. Initial cohort studies reported mortality ranging from 39% to 61%. A pharmacovigilance study reported a lower incident risk of CVT after mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccines than after adenovirus-based vaccines (1–5/10000 for BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 versus 13/10000 for ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine); it found no evidence of VITT after mRNA vaccines.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Suspected VITT calls for platelet factor 4 antibody testing and management by a hematologist and multidisciplinary team. Despite limited evidence, avoidance of heparin products, intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg body weight daily for 2 days, and steroids have been advised. Platelet transfusions are not recommended. Nonheparin parenteral anticoagulants, typically argatroban or fondaparinux, are used initially, with a switch to an oral anticoagulant such as a DOAC after full platelet-count recovery.

special_populations.considerations: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is a recognized CVT risk factor. Patients with this syndrome were excluded from the cited ACTION-CVT and SECRET studies. In individuals with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, DOACs have been associated with more recurrent thromboembolic events than warfarin.

Active cancer is associated with poorer CVT prognosis. Patients with malignancy were excluded from the cited ACTION-CVT and RE-SPECT CVT studies. For cancer-associated VTE, the statement reports that DOACs were at least noninferior to LMWH for prevention; it does not establish that finding specifically for CVT.
Severe renal failure may preclude gadolinium administration when venous imaging is needed.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: TOF MRV can be used when gadolinium administration is precluded.

special_populations.considerations: Oral contraception and hormonal therapies, chiefly estrogen-based formulations, may increase the odds of CVT nearly 8-fold; obesity may add a synergistic effect. The listed predisposing conditions also include hormone therapy for transfeminine or transmasculine individuals.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) accounts for 0.5% to 3% of strokes. Young people, women of reproductive age, and people with prothrombotic states are particularly vulnerable. Symptoms vary and include headache and seizures, so diagnosis requires substantial clinical suspicion. Diagnosis relies chiefly on magnetic resonance imaging with magnetic resonance venography or computed tomography with computed tomographic venography. The course can be unpredictable; despite intensive medical care, 10% to 15% of patients die or become dependent. This statement updates the 2011 American Heart Association statement, concentrating on diagnostic advances and decisions about anticoagulation, endovascular treatment, and craniectomy. It also presents an approach to management when neurological status worsens or a thrombus extends despite maximal medical treatment.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis and Management of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
document_sections.content: CVT means a thrombus in the dural venous sinuses, cerebral veins, or both, and represents 0.5% to 3% of strokes. Registries and cohorts suggest that it chiefly affects people <55 years of age; two-thirds of cases occur in women. Outcomes are generally favorable, and most patients survive without physical disability, although persistent symptoms that diminish quality of life are not unusual. Older age, active cancer, reduced consciousness, and intracerebral hemorrhage are among the commonly reported markers of poor prognosis. The statement covers symptoms, predisposing factors, developments in imaging and treatment, and management in pediatric patients, during pregnancy and the puerperium, and in vaccine-induced CVT. It incorporates evidence published since the 2011 statement and identifies subjects for future research.

document_sections.heading: CLINICAL PRESENTATION
document_sections.content: Symptoms can result from raised intracranial pressure or focal parenchymal damage, whether or not mass effect is present. Headache occurs in nearly 90% of cases and is the commonest symptom. Other manifestations related to intracranial pressure include nausea, transient visual obscurations or vision loss (13%–27%), papilledema, diplopia (6%–14%), and other cranial neuropathies (6%–11%). Approximately 20% to 40% of patients present with seizures, 20% to 50% with focal neurological deficits, and up to 20% with encephalopathy or coma. Onset is generally less abrupt than with other stroke types; most patients present >48 hours after symptoms begin. A minority have thunderclap headache or subarachnoid hemorrhage (<5%), or sudden focal deficits (5%–40%). Additional presentation details are summarized in Supplemental Table 1.

document_sections.heading: LONG-TERM SYMPTOMS AND CVT RECURRENCE
document_sections.content: Functional independence, defined as a modified Rankin Scale score of 0–2, is achieved by 80% to 90% of patients. Nevertheless, studies describe frequent residual problems with cognition, mood, fatigue, and headache that can prevent a return to previous activities. In a prospective cohort from a Canadian randomized trial, 72% were functionally independent at presentation, yet headache, fatigue, low mood, and impaired cognitive performance imposed a substantial burden. In a retrospective Chinese study of 303 people employed or studying before CVT, 42% had not resumed work or school at 6 months, although 87% were functionally independent when assessed. Epilepsy may develop in >10%; reported risk factors include seizures at onset, diminished consciousness or focal deficits, baseline hemorrhagic lesions or superior sagittal sinus involvement, and craniectomy. Dural arteriovenous fistula has been reported both as a complication and as a condition preceding CVT. A retrospective series of 1218 patients reported newly detected dural arteriovenous fistula in 2.4% at a median follow-up of 8 months (interquartile range, 5–23 months), but had no systematic imaging schedule or protocol. A prospective study with standardized imaging at 6 months detected no dural arteriovenous fistula. After CVT, recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) occurs at 1% to 4% per year; reported CVT recurrence is generally <1% to 2% per year. Severe thrombophilia, including malignancy, previous VTE, and an event without an identified precipitant have been linked to greater recurrence risk; findings concerning male sex have been inconsistent. A secondary ACTION-CVT analysis reported VTE recurrence of 6.4%, including 2.5% for CVT recurrence alone, although brain images were not centrally adjudicated. A recent retrospective study found recurrent VTE, including CVT, at 5.68 per 100 patient-years; more than half of those recurrences were CVT. A Norwegian study of patients with CVT (n=654; median age, 41 years; 67% women) found higher risks of recurrent VTE, ischemic stroke, major bleeding, and death at 10 years than in age- and sex-matched general-population controls. The excess recurrent-VTE risk was greater at age 18–54 years, whereas ischemic stroke, major bleeding, and mortality risks were greatest in older patients; the reported mortality risk difference was 11.5% for women ≥55 years of age and 5.8% for men ≥55 years.

document_sections.heading: PREDISPOSING FACTORS
document_sections.content: Most patients have an identifiable predisposing factor, which can be temporary or persistent. The accompanying table groups these factors and medical conditions by whether they are transient or chronic; its percentages describe their presence among patients with CVT and can total >100% because patients may have >1 condition. Rates are highest among younger women. Oral contraception and pregnancy or the puerperium are major risks. Oral contraceptives and hormonal therapies, especially estrogen-based preparations, may raise the odds of CVT nearly 8-fold; obesity may add a synergistic effect. Established associations also include antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, JAK2 mutations, cancer—particularly myeloproliferative disorders—and autoimmune conditions such as Behçet and inflammatory bowel disease. Protein C and protein S deficiency, factor V Leiden, and prothrombin G20210A polymorphism are additional genetic thrombophilias associated with CVT. Reported temporary triggers include COVID-19 and head and neck infections, dehydration, corticosteroids, l-asparaginase, and vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT). Head trauma, neurosurgical procedures, and lesions such as meningiomas that compress venous sinuses are also associated with CVT.

document_sections.heading: BRAIN AND VASCULAR IMAGING FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF CVT
document_sections.content: Conventional computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is often obtained first for nonspecific acute symptoms. Suspicion can arise from direct thrombus visualization, absent venous filling, tissue consequences of venous obstruction—venous infarction, edema, hemorrhagic transformation, intracranial hypertension, or hydrocephalus—or vascular consequences such as enlarged veins. Supplemental Table 2 summarizes imaging difficulties. Thin-slice CT can improve direct visualization. On noncontrast CT, increased hemoglobin and red blood cells within a thrombus produce hyperattenuation, termed the dense vessel sign. A serpiginous or linear venous hyperdensity, described as the cord or string sign, or a dense triangle sign can remain visible up to 14 days after symptom onset. Indirect CT and MRI clues include low-density areas that do not follow a usual wedge-shaped infarct pattern or arterial territory, or that spare the overlying cortex. Sagittal sinus or deep cerebral vein involvement can produce bilateral hypodensities. Hemorrhage occurs in up to 40% of patients and may represent hemorrhagic transformation within a hypodense area or intracerebral hemorrhage accompanied by subarachnoid or subdural bleeding; isolated subarachnoid and basal ganglia hemorrhages are uncommon. A juxtacortical C-shaped hyperdensity, the cashew nut sign, has reportedly high specificity but low sensitivity. Bilateral or multifocal hemorrhage is also frequent. A meta-analysis covering 27 publications and 2812 cases estimated CT sensitivity at 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity at 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91), below the figures previously described in the 2011 American Heart Association statement. Conventional MRI can show the thrombus directly, but its signal changes with thrombus age as oxyhemoglobin becomes deoxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin. Early thrombus can be isointense or hypointense on T2 and resemble a normal sinus flow void, complicating diagnosis. Time-of-flight magnetic resonance venography (MRV) can likewise mislead when absent flow is not confirmed on T1//T2. Corroboration using gradient-recalled echo, susceptibility-weighted imaging, or contrast-enhanced MRV is often useful. Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact on gradient-recalled echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences; for subtle cortical vein thrombosis, their sensitivity and specificity approach 100%. T1-based black-blood imaging is described as promising. MRI detects parenchymal injury secondary to venous occlusion more sensitively than CT; resulting lesions can be bilateral and cross arterial territories. A meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 1773 patients with CVT estimated sensitivity of conventional MRI sequences at 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity at 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94). The figures illustrate venous-system anatomy and sinus involvement, examples of thrombosis and hemorrhage on noncontrast CT, and venous thrombosis, infarction, edema, and filling defects on MRI. Sinus-involvement percentages in the anatomy figure may exceed 100% because >1 sinus can be affected; internal jugular vein thrombosis there refers to its coexistence with CVT, not isolated jugular thrombosis.

document_sections.heading: CONFIRMING THE DIAGNOSIS OF CVT
document_sections.content: CT venography (CTV) and MRV are the preferred confirmatory examinations. Digital subtraction angiography is generally reserved for situations in which an invasive intervention is contemplated. CTV displays superficial and deep cerebral veins; thrombi usually appear as filling defects, including the empty delta sign in the superior sagittal sinus, and can generally be distinguished from arachnoid granulations. Several small or moderately sized studies found high CTV sensitivity and specificity against digital subtraction angiography or a consensus interpretation of other studies. CTV is less sensitive than MRI for cortical vein thrombosis. MRV can use noncontrast time-of-flight (TOF), phase-contrast, or contrast-enhanced acquisition. Gadolinium-enhanced MRV directly depicts luminal filling and increases sensitivity for thrombi in smaller veins. TOF and phase-contrast studies can both have artifacts from complex flow. TOF remains widely used and is particularly useful when gadolinium may be unsuitable, including during pregnancy or breastfeeding and in severe renal failure. In slow flow, 2-dimensional TOF is more sensitive than 3-dimensional TOF. Phase-contrast MRI is used less often because choosing its velocity-encoding parameter is difficult and operator dependent and acquisition takes longer. Contrast-enhanced MRV has sensitivity and specificity comparable to CTV and better distinguishes slow flow from a hypoplastic sinus or flow gaps. Contrast-enhanced MRV, gradient-recalled echo, or susceptibility-weighted imaging is recommended when diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis; this represents evidence added since the 2011 American Heart Association statement.

document_sections.heading: THERAPEUTIC ADVANCES IN THE MANAGEMENT OF CVT
document_sections.content: The statement examines oral anticoagulation, reperfusion interventions, and decompressive craniectomy. The proposed management figure summarizes an approach to CVT diagnosis and treatment, but its decision steps are not specified in its caption.

document_sections.heading: Oral Anticoagulation
document_sections.content: Anticoagulation aims to stop thrombus extension, promote recanalization, and prevent recurrent VTE. Earlier American Heart Association/American Stroke Association and European guidance recommended initially choosing low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) rather than unfractionated heparin, followed by an oral vitamin K antagonist (VKA) for 3 to 12 months when risk factors are transient, or indefinitely when major thrombotic risk factors persist or VTE recurs. LMWH is favored for acute CVT because administration is more practical, its anticoagulant effect is more predictable, and thrombocytopenia risk is lower; meta-analyses also show trends toward better outcomes that do not meet the threshold for statistical significance. Venous hemorrhage is not a contraindication to anticoagulation. Whether recanalization should determine treatment duration remains uncertain. Emerging evidence suggests direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) may be a reasonable oral alternative for selected patients. ACTION-CVT retrospectively compared 845 consecutive patients prescribed a VKA or DOAC in routine care between 2015 and 2020. Among DOAC users, treatments included apixaban (67%), rivaroxaban (18%), dabigatran (14%), or multiple DOACs (3%). Patients with cancer, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, or pregnancy were excluded. Recurrent VTE did not differ significantly (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.15– 1.73]); major hemorrhage risk was lower with DOACs (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.35 [95% CI, 0.15–0.82]), principally because intracerebral hemorrhage was less frequent. Recanalization rates did not differ between treatment groups in either study cited for this comparison. A systematic review of 3 randomized trials and 16 observational studies comparing DOACs with VKAs found similar recurrent-VTE and major-hemorrhage rates and similar complete recanalization (42.9% versus 42.3%; relative risk, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87–1.11]). RE-SPECT CVT randomized 120 patients with CVT 1:1 to warfarin, targeting an international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0, or dabigatran 150 mg twice daily for 6 months after 5 to 15 days of parenteral anticoagulation. It excluded cancer, central nervous system infection, trauma, and pregnancy. Neither group had recurrent VTE. Major hemorrhage occurred in 1 dabigatran recipient (1.7% [95% CI, 0.0%–8.9%]; gastrointestinal bleeding) and 2 warfarin recipients (3.3% [95% CI, 0.4%–11.5%]; both intracerebral hemorrhages). SECRET, a phase II study, randomized 53 participants with CVT 1:1 to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily or standard anticoagulation—warfarin targeting an international normalized ratio of 2.0–3.0 or LMWH—for a minimum of 6 months. Parenteral anticoagulation before study treatment was not required. Pregnancy and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome were exclusion criteria; 19 of 26 rivaroxaban recipients nonetheless received ≤4 days of initial parenteral anticoagulation. The study reported no safety concern with early DOAC initiation. At 6 months, its rivaroxaban group had 1 recurrent CVT (3.8% [95% CI, 0.1%–19.6%]), 1 symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (3.8% [95% CI, 0.1%–19.6%]), and 2 clinically relevant nonmajor bleeds (7.7% [95% CI, 0.9%–25.1%]); the control group had no recurrent VTE or bleeding events. On currently available evidence, transition to either a DOAC or a VKA after initial parenteral anticoagulation is reasonable, but it is unknown whether an initial period of 5 to 15 days is safer or more effective than a shorter period. Further trials and prospective observational work are ongoing (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03178864, NCT04660747). Unresolved questions include when to begin oral therapy with or without preceding heparin, whether initial acute-VTE dosing is needed, and which patients are appropriate DOAC candidates. During pregnancy, DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated and only LMWH is recommended; DOACs are also contraindicated during breastfeeding. In antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, DOACs have been associated with more recurrent thromboembolic events than warfarin. For cancer-associated VTE prevention, DOACs were at least noninferior to LMWH. Evidence concerning antiplatelet treatment after oral anticoagulation ends in CVT is limited. In VTE secondary-prevention studies, aspirin outperformed placebo (hazard ratio, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.51–0.90]; P=0.008). Because people with CVT are younger than the broader VTE population, potential aspirin exposure would last longer; evidence on their long-term recurrence is also less robust. Potential benefits therefore warrant consideration alongside individual characteristics through shared decision-making.

document_sections.heading: Reperfusion Therapies
document_sections.content: Endovascular treatment (EVT) could theoretically restore venous flow faster, but whether it improves outcomes over medical care, particularly in an unselected population, is uncertain. Reports on balloon-assisted thrombectomy, aspiration or vacuum aspiration, intrasinus thrombolysis alone or combined with thrombectomy, intra-arterial thrombolysis, and intrasinus stenting provide conflicting evidence on safety and complications. In the multicenter randomized TO-ACT trial, patients with severe CVT did not gain a clinical benefit from EVT compared with standard anticoagulation. Larger studies and meta-analyses associated EVT with higher mortality and found no evidence of benefit. Currently, EVT is used as rescue treatment when patients deteriorate clinically, standard treatment fails, or standard treatment is contraindicated. A systematic review of 10 studies involving 339 EVT-treated patients reported complete or partial recanalization in 90.0% after the procedure and 95.2% during follow-up; complications occurred in 10.3%. Current evidence does not establish that any particular EVT technique, including stent retrievers, microcatheters, aspiration catheters, or aspiration pump systems, is superior to another therapeutic strategy.

document_sections.heading: Decompressive Craniectomy
document_sections.content: Evidence for decompressive craniectomy has not changed since the earlier American Heart Association statement. It should be offered as a potentially lifesaving treatment to patients with acute severe CVT, parenchymal lesions, and impending herniation. Age >50 years, midline shift >10 mm, and complete effacement of the basal cisterns have been associated with worse outcomes. No randomized controlled trial of this operation was identified. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 studies including 483 patients with CVT suggested that surgery within 48 hours of admission may reduce mortality (odds ratio [OR], 0.26 [95% CI, 0.10–0.69]) and improve functional outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Population
document_sections.content: CVT is more frequent in neonates (6.4/100000) than in older children and adolescents. Prompt consideration of the diagnosis is important when a child acutely develops headache, seizures, focal deficits, or coma, or has circumstances such as sepsis—including mastoiditis, Lemierre syndrome, COVID-19, or meningitis—head trauma, including abuse, hypoxia, or dehydration. Particular vigilance is warranted with congenital heart disease or its surgical treatment, cancer or its treatment, iron-deficiency anemia or hemoglobinopathies, and inflammatory diseases such as nephrotic syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease. Emergency imaging to establish or exclude dural or cortical venous thrombosis, with or without parenchymal damage or hemorrhage, typically requires anesthesia. Initial blood testing may identify low platelets associated with platelet factor 4 mutations; elevated platelets and hemoglobin associated with JAK2 mutations; or signs of iron deficiency, whether or not anemia is present. Acute management generally uses LMWH or unfractionated heparin. As in adults, worsening consciousness may justify considering more invasive, potentially lifesaving procedures. Acute anticoagulation in premature and term neonates is more controversial but is reasonable: evidence of posttreatment hemorrhage is lacking, whereas withholding anticoagulation may permit thrombus extension. Pediatric CVT mortality is 3%; recurrent venous thrombosis occurs in ≈6% and is usually associated with absent anticoagulation and lack of venous recanalization. Trials published since the earlier statement have examined treatment duration and DOACs. Kids-DOTT studied individuals 4 months to 20.9 years of age with provoked VTE, including 59/417; 25% patients with CVT, and compared 6 weeks with 3 months of anticoagulation. The 6-week course was noninferior for recurrent VTE and bleeding. In EINSTEIN-Jr, after initial heparinization, 114 children with confirmed CVT were randomized 2:1 to 3 months of rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulation with continued heparin or a switch to an oral VKA. Its main efficacy measure was symptomatic recurrent VTE; its principal safety measure was major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding. Follow-up was 100%. Symptomatic recurrent VTE occurred in none of the 73 rivaroxaban-treated children and 1 of the 41 standard-treatment children (absolute difference, 2.4% [95% CI, −2.6% to 13.5%]). Five rivaroxaban recipients experienced nonmajor, noncerebral bleeding, while 1 standard-treatment recipient had a major subdural bleed. Complete and partial recanalization occurred, respectively, in 18 (25%) and 39 (53%) rivaroxaban recipients and 6 (15%) and 24 (59%) standard-treatment recipients. No child died during the 3-month treatment period. At study end, focal deficits affected 5 (6.8%) children receiving rivaroxaban and 3 (7.3%) receiving standard anticoagulation. Other long-term studies suggest that, despite treatment, 1 in 4 children may develop late epilepsy; infantile spasms after neonatal CVT, cognitive impairment, and intracranial hypertension are also reported.

document_sections.heading: CVT During Pregnancy and Puerperium
document_sections.content: Pregnancy-related changes in coagulation continue into the puerperium and create a hypercoagulable state that raises CVT risk. Estimates for pregnancy and puerperium in Western countries range from 1 in 2500 deliveries to 1 in 10000 deliveries; reported ORs span 1.3 to 13.0. Risk is greatest in the third trimester and first 6 postpartum weeks, with approximately 80% of pregnancy-related cases occurring after delivery. One case-control study detected increased risk only in the puerperium (OR, 10.6 [95% CI, 5.6–20.0]); its estimate during pregnancy was not statistically significant (OR, 1.2 [95% CI, 0.6–2.3]). Cesarean delivery appeared associated with greater risk after adjustment for age, vascular risks, infection, hospital type, and location (OR, 3.10 [95% CI, 2.26–4.24]). Studies since the previous statement have generally found prognosis in pregnancy-related CVT to be at least as favorable as in CVT overall. VKAs, including warfarin, are contraindicated during pregnancy because of fetal embryopathy and fetal or neonatal bleeding. Consequently, most women with CVT during pregnancy and early puerperium receive LMWH. Evidence on endovascular interventions in this population is limited. As outside pregnancy, thrombolysis and thrombectomy are reserved for neurological deterioration or thrombus propagation despite medical therapy.

document_sections.heading: Future Pregnancies and Recurrence
document_sections.content: Women with prior VTE appear to face increased risk of thrombotic events, including deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, in later pregnancies. A systematic review of 17 studies encompassing 393 pregnancies estimated recurrent CVT at 8 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 3–22) and noncerebral VTE at 22 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 11–43). It observed a trend toward fewer recurrent thrombotic events among women using antithrombotic prophylaxis. Available evidence does not identify previous CVT as a contraindication to another pregnancy. Given the added pregnancy-related risk, LMWH prophylaxis during future pregnancies and after delivery is probably beneficial.

document_sections.heading: VITT and CVT
document_sections.content: Reports in 2021 described thrombocytopenia with CVT after the adenovirus-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccines ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca) and Ad26.COV2.S (Janssen). Affected patients were 18 to 77 years old and predominantly women; symptoms started 5 to 24 days after vaccination. Headache was the leading presenting symptom, and all reported patients had thrombocytopenia. A United Kingdom report described 23 patients with platelet factor 4 antibodies following ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccination. It has been proposed that DNA from adenovirus-infected cells binds platelet factor 4 and provokes autoantibody production. CVT associated with VITT is rare but had a poor prognosis in initial cohorts, with mortality of 39% to 61%. In a study of 2313 CVT admissions spanning 1 prepandemic year (2019) and 1 pandemic year (2020), 26 patients had VITT and 6 of them died; COVID-19 infection was diagnosed in 7.6% of all CVT admissions. A pharmacovigilance analysis of >1.7 million adverse-reaction reports found a disproportionately lower incident risk of CVT with mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccines than with adenovirus-based vaccination (1–5/10000 for BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 versus 13/10000 for ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine). Evidence of VITT after mRNA vaccination was not found. Suspected VITT warrants testing for platelet factor 4 antibodies. Despite limited evidence, the similarity to autoimmune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia has led to advice to avoid heparin products and give intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg body weight daily for 2 days and steroids. Platelet transfusion is not recommended. Nonheparin parenteral anticoagulants, usually argatroban or fondaparinux, are typically used first; transition to an oral anticoagulant such as a DOAC follows full platelet-count recovery.

document_sections.heading: KEY POINTS FOR CLINICAL PRACTICE
document_sections.content: Consider CVT with substantial clinical suspicion when common symptoms coexist with pregnancy, the puerperium, oral contraceptive use, thrombophilia, or demographic factors such as being a young woman. Obesity, COVID-19, and vaccine-induced thrombocytopenia are predisposing conditions highlighted since the prior report. MRI/MRV is recommended as the noninvasive confirmatory examination of cerebral veins; CT/CTV is a reasonable alternative where resources are limited or pretest probability is low. For cortical vein thrombosis, contrast-enhanced MRV, gradient-recalled echo, or susceptibility-weighted imaging is recommended. Standard initial treatment comprises parenteral heparin followed by an oral VKA for 3 to 12 months according to cause, or indefinitely when thrombophilia or recurrent VTE is present. Open-label retrospective and prospective randomized studies suggest DOACs are a safe and effective alternative to VKAs. Whether follow-up CTV or MRV evidence of recanalization should determine anticoagulation duration is uncertain. Given the lack of controlled evidence and poorer outcomes in meta-analyses, endovascular treatment is reserved for thrombus extension, neurological deterioration despite medical treatment, or contraindications to anticoagulation. Despite limited evidence, decompressive surgery may save life and improve function when clinical signs of herniation are advanced. For CVT during pregnancy, full-dose LMWH should continue throughout pregnancy; LMWH or a VKA targeting an international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 should then continue for at least 6 weeks postpartum, with total treatment lasting at least 3 months. It is reasonable to tell women with previous CVT that another pregnancy is not contraindicated; LMWH prophylaxis during future pregnancy and the postpartum period is usually recommended. Pediatric CVT is more common in neonates than in older children and often occurs with infection, dehydration, iron deficiency, anemia, or head trauma. First-line treatment is parenteral anticoagulation, followed by LMWH, a VKA, or rivaroxaban for at least 6 weeks. Rare VITT-associated CVT can arise days or weeks after adenovirus-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, generally with a new headache and thrombocytopenia, and requires specialist hematology and multidisciplinary management.
